parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description:
Send one on every write. A retry carrying the same key returns the FIRST response instead of doing the work twice — without it, a client that times out and retries schedules the post a second time, and the first is already queued.

Any string up to 255 characters; a UUID per logical operation is the usual choice. Keys are scoped to your workspace and honoured for 24 hours. The same key with a different body is a `422`; a request still running under this key is a `409 request_in_progress`.

What a FAILED request does to its key depends on whether it could have changed anything. A `4xx` releases it — every one of them is raised before we write a thing, so fix the input and retry with the same key. A `5xx` pins it, and the retry replays that failure instead of doing the work: a write is several posts and several workflows, so a fault partway through leaves some of them done, and a fresh attempt would publish those a second time. Read `GET /posts/{id}` to see what exists, then continue with a new key.

post.description:
One call, one submission, however many channels. Sending this once per channel instead produces that many unrelated submissions, each with its own id and schedule.

`intent: "now"` is **asynchronous** — the response comes back `publishing`, not published. Poll `GET /posts/{id}` for the outcome.

Every channel is validated against its own platform’s rules — and your allowance checked — before anything is written. So a REFUSAL is total: a `4xx` here created nothing, and there is no state where two of four channels exist because the third had a typo.

The write itself is one transaction, so a database failure is total too — there is no half-written submission.

SCHEDULING is where the channels stop being one thing: each gets its own workflow, and an outage while starting the fourth must not unschedule three that are already correct. So a submission where some channels started comes back **2xx with the failures per channel** — that channel reads `failed` and carries the reason — rather than as a blanket error. Retry it by sending the submission again to `PUT /posts/{id}`, which reschedules the failed channels without duplicating the ones that worked. Only a submission where EVERY channel failed to start is a `503`.

Send an `Idempotency-Key` regardless: on that `503` the retry replays the failure instead of creating the submission twice, and `GET /posts` shows what exists.

Send one on every write. A retry carrying the same key returns the FIRST response instead of doing the work twice — without it, a client that times out and retries schedules the post a second time, and the first is already queued.

Any string up to 255 characters; a UUID per logical operation is the usual choice. Keys are scoped to your workspace and honoured for 24 hours. The same key with a different body is a `422`; a request still running under this key is a `409 request_in_progress`.

What a FAILED request does to its key depends on whether it could have changed anything. A `4xx` releases it — every one of them is raised before we write a thing, so fix the input and retry with the same key. A `5xx` pins it, and the retry replays that failure instead of doing the work: a write is several posts and several workflows, so a fault partway through leaves some of them done, and a fresh attempt would publish those a second time. Read `GET /posts/{id}` to see what exists, then continue with a new key.

get.description:
Every reading the sweep has stored for this submission, per channel, oldest first. `GET /public/v1/stats` sums the LATEST reading of many publications over a window; this is every reading of one.

THE POINTS ARE NOT EVENLY SPACED. Sampling decays: roughly hourly for the first day, daily for a week, weekly out to thirty days, then it stops for good. Plot against `capturedAt` and never against the index, and read a month-old post as frozen at its last reading rather than as having stopped earning.

AN ABSENT METRIC IS NOT A ZERO, exactly as on `/stats`. A key missing from a reading’s `values` was not reported at that capture — most platforms simply do not measure most metrics.

A channel with an empty `readings` is the normal case, not an error, and this endpoint deliberately does not say which of the three reasons applies: the platform reports nothing to us, the connection was authorized before we asked for the read permission, or the post has not been swept yet. All three are facts about the CHANNEL — join `channelId` against `metricsStatus` on `GET /public/v1/channels`.

ANALYTICS, NOT BILLING. These are counted from the posts themselves, so deleting a post changes the history: the figures can go down. Use `GET /public/v1/usage` for anything commercial — it reads the meter an invoice is computed from, and it is the only endpoint that predicts a `402`.

`totals`, `daily`, `channels` and `tags` describe the window. `queue` is a snapshot of right now and ignores `from`/`to` entirely.

Every channel connected right now appears in `channels`, including those that published nothing. Publications whose account has since been disconnected collect in a single row with a null `channelId`, so the per-channel figures always sum to `totals`.

`tags` behaves differently on purpose, and the difference matters: only tags something landed under appear, and the counts OVERLAP. A publication carrying two tags is counted under both, one carrying none under neither — so unlike `channels`, these do not sum to `totals` and must not be rendered as shares of it.

ENGAGEMENT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF NUMBER from everything above. `engagement` on the response, and on each channel and tag, is what the PLATFORMS reported back — likes, comments, shares and whatever else each one measures — rather than something counted from our own rows. 1. It is PARTIAL. 3. The values are CUMULATIVE and still moving. Each is the latest reading of a publication since it went out — not what it earned during the window — and it changes when somebody likes or unlikes the post. Readings are sampled for roughly the first month of a post’s life and then stop.

info.title: Bulkit API
info.description:
Schedule and publish social media posts programmatically.

## The model

One call to `POST /posts` creates a **submission**: one piece of content sent to one or
more connected channels. It is a single resource with a single id, and every
`/posts/{id}` route addresses it.

Inside it, each channel publishes **independently** — its own status, its own error,
its own retry. That is deliberate: an outage at X cannot hold up LinkedIn. So a
submission can come back `partially_published`, and the per-channel entries in
`channels[]` are where the real outcome lives.

Each channel carries **blocks**: one is an ordinary post, several is a thread (a chain
of tweets, a LinkedIn post and its comments). Blocks publish one at a time and each is
confirmed as it lands, which is what lets a retry resume at block four instead of
re-posting the whole chain.

> Call `POST /posts` **once** with several entries in `channels[]`. Calling it once per
> channel produces several unrelated submissions, each with its own id and schedule.

## Before you start

**You need your own platform credentials.** Bulkit publishes through your
workspace’s own X / LinkedIn / Meta applications, which you register and get
approved with each platform, then connect in the Bulkit app. That approval is days to
weeks of work with the platforms themselves and it is a hard prerequisite: an API key
alone cannot post anything. Connect at least one channel in the app first, then come
back here.

Connecting an account is not on this API and cannot be — it is an interactive OAuth
flow that ends in a browser redirect, so it has no meaning for a machine caller.

## Authentication

Every route requires an API key, minted under **API** in the app and shown exactly
once. Send it either way — they are equivalent:

```http
x-api-key: bk_live_...
Authorization: Bearer bk_live_...
```

**Scopes.** A key is `read` or `read+write`. A read-only key gets `403 forbidden` on
anything that changes state, including `POST /posts/{id}/publish` — publishing is a
write no matter which verb it uses.

**Test mode.** A key is either live (`bk_live_...`) or test (`bk_test_...`), and the
prefix is there so you can tell which one is in a `.env` at a glance. A test key
validates, stores and refuses exactly as a live one does — same platform rules, same
quota check, same error for the same mistake — but starts no publishing workflow and
records nothing on your bill. It is the safe way to build against this API without
posting to a real account.

## Quickstart

```bash
# 1. What can I post to?
curl -H "x-api-key: $BULKIT_KEY" \
  https://your-instance/public/v1/channels

# 2. What will each platform accept?
curl -H "x-api-key: $BULKIT_KEY" \
  https://your-instance/public/v1/platforms

# 3. Schedule one thing to two channels.
curl -X POST \
  -H "x-api-key: $BULKIT_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  https://your-instance/public/v1/posts \
  -d '{
    "intent": "schedule",
    "scheduledAt": "2026-09-01T09:00:00Z",
    "channels": [
      { "channelId": "chn_x", "blocks": [{ "content": "Shipping today." }] },
      { "channelId": "chn_li", "blocks": [{ "content": "A longer version, for LinkedIn." }] }
    ]
  }'
```

## Publishing is asynchronous

`intent: "now"` queues the submission and returns; it does **not** wait for the
platforms. The response comes back `publishing`, and the outcome arrives minutes later
— or days later, for a scheduled post. Anything else would hold an HTTP request open
for as long as a five-block thread takes and time out on exactly the submissions that
matter most.

Register a **webhook** and the outcome is pushed to you instead — see below. Polling
`GET /posts/{id}` still works and is the right fallback, but a client that polls for a
post scheduled next Tuesday spends a request a minute for a week to learn one fact.

## Webhooks

Register a URL with `POST /webhooks` and we POST each event to it as it happens. The
response to that call carries the **signing secret** — store it then, because only an
encrypted copy is kept and no route returns it.

| Event | When |
| --- | --- |
| `post.published` | every block of one channel’s post is live |
| `post.failed` | one channel’s post did not go out, and nothing of it is live |
| `post.partially_failed` | a thread died partway: some blocks are live, the rest are not |
| `channel.needs_reconnect` | an account can no longer publish without a human re-authorizing it |

The `post.*` events fire **once per channel**, not once per submission. That follows
from the model above: each channel publishes independently, so there is no single moment
at which "the submission" published. `data.channelId` says which one, and `data.post` is
the whole submission in the shape `GET /posts/{id}` returns — so an ordinary subscriber
never has to call back.

### Verifying a delivery

Your URL is reachable by anyone on the internet. An unverified handler acts on whatever
a stranger posts to it, so this is not optional:

```http
POST /your/endpoint
x-bulkit-signature: t=1755432000,v1=6f1a…
x-bulkit-event-id: 0f9c8e2a-…
x-bulkit-event-type: post.published
x-bulkit-attempt: 1
```

The signature is `HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<t>.<raw body>")`, hex. Verify with the **raw**
body — not a re-serialization of the parsed JSON, whose key order and whitespace will
differ and produce a different digest. Then check `t` against your own clock and reject
anything older than ~5 minutes; the timestamp is inside the signed material precisely so a
captured delivery cannot be replayed forever.

```js
const signed = `${t}.${rawBody}`;
const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(signed).digest("hex");
const ok = crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(v1));
```

Compare in constant time. A `===` on hex digests leaks, through timing, how many leading
characters of a guess were right.

### Delivery, retries and duplicates

Delivery is **at-least-once**. A receiver that returns 200 after its own timeout will be
sent the event again, so treat `id` in the body (also `x-bulkit-event-id`) as the dedupe
key — it is stable across every redelivery of one fact.

Return a 2xx quickly and do the work afterwards. Anything else is retried with
exponential backoff — 10s, 20s, 40s … capped hourly, for about five hours. Only a 2xx
counts: redirects are **not** followed, because a 3xx would move the delivery to an
address you never registered.

`GET /webhooks/{id}/deliveries` is the record of every attempt — status, our description
of the failure, and how long it took. Your response body is never stored or returned.

An endpoint whose deliveries fail for five consecutive events is **disabled**
automatically, with the reason on the endpoint. Fix the receiver and re-enable it with
`PUT /webhooks/{id}` — which also clears the failure streak, so you are not one flake
away from being switched off again.

### Test mode

A test key writes posts but starts no publishing workflow, and webhooks fire from that
workflow — so **a test key produces no events**. To check a receiver is wired up and
verifying signatures, send it a `webhook.test` event with `POST /webhooks/{id}/test`, which
works with either kind of key. To exercise it end to end, use a live key against a channel
you do not mind posting to.

## Idempotency

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on every write. A retry carrying the same key returns
the **first** response instead of doing the work again. Without one, a client that
times out and retries schedules the post a second time — and the first one is already
queued, so the duplicate is not a duplicate row, it is a duplicate tweet.

Keys are scoped to your workspace, honoured for 24 hours, and up to 255 characters
(a UUID per logical operation is the usual choice). The same key with a different body
is a `422`; a request still running under the key is a `409 request_in_progress`.

What a **failed** request does to its key turns on one question — could it have changed
anything before it failed?

- **`4xx` releases the key.** Every one of them is raised before a row is written, so fix
  the input and retry with the same key.
- **`5xx` keeps it, and the retry replays that same failure.** One write is several posts
  and several publishing workflows, so a fault partway through leaves some of them done.
  A retry that started over would publish those a second time — which is the duplicate this
  header exists to prevent, arriving by the other road. Read `GET /posts/{id}` to see what
  exists, then carry on with a new key.

## Pagination

`GET /posts` is cursor-paginated. Pass `nextCursor` from the previous page as `?cursor=`,
and stop when it comes back `null` — an empty `data` is not the signal.

Default page size is 25 and the ceiling is 100; asking for more is clamped rather
than refused. Cursors are opaque strings: they name a position in the ordering, not an
offset, so pages stay correct while posts are being created and published underneath
you. Do not parse or construct one.

## Rate limits

Limited **per API key**, at the ceiling your plan bought, across the whole API — one
bucket, not one per route. Every response carries:

| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `X-RateLimit-Limit` | Requests allowed per minute |
| `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Left in the current window |
| `X-RateLimit-Reset` | Seconds until it refills |

A `429` carries them too, plus `Retry-After`. Requests that arrive without a usable key
are limited to 20 a minute per IP — every route here needs one, so a request without
it is a misconfigured client or someone probing.

## Quotas are not rate limits

These look alike and behaving as if they were the same is the most expensive mistake a
client can make here:

- **`429 rate_limited`** — you are going too fast. Back off and retry; `Retry-After` says
  when. No upgrade needed.
- **`402 quota_exceeded`** — your plan’s allowance for the period is spent. Retrying will
  never succeed. `GET /usage` has the numbers and `periodEnd` is when they reset.

A client that retries a `402` backs off forever against a limit that moves once a month.

## Stats are not usage

Two endpoints return numbers about your workspace, from two different sources, and they
are not interchangeable:

- **`GET /usage`** reads an append-only meter. It is what a bill is computed from, it only
  rises within a period, and it is the only endpoint that predicts a `402`.
- **`GET /stats`** counts the posts themselves. Delete a post and last month changes —
  normal for analytics, disqualifying for an invoice.

So never poll `/stats` to decide whether the next write will be refused: those figures can
go down, and none of them is a ceiling.

## Errors

Every failure arrives in one envelope:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "content_too_long",
    "message": "X (Twitter) allows 280 characters — this one is 300",
    "field": "channels[1].blocks[0].content",
    "requestId": "req_a8b0c1d2-3e4f-5678-9abc-def012345678"
  }
}
```

Branch on `code`. `message` is the best explanation we have and is safe to show your own
users, but it is prose and will change. `field` points into the request body you sent —
or names the header at fault, for the failures a header produces.

Every failure arrives this way, including the ones raised before your request reaches a
route: an unparseable body, a body over the size ceiling, a path or method that does not
exist. There is no second error shape to write a parser for.

When schema validation rejects more than one field, all of them come back together in
`details`, so a client fixes them in one pass instead of a round trip per mistake:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "invalid_request",
    "message": "channels[0].channelId must be a string; channels[0].blocks[1].content must be a string",
    "field": "channels[0].channelId",
    "details": [
      { "field": "channels[0].channelId", "message": "channels[0].channelId must be a string" },
      { "field": "channels[0].blocks[1].content", "message": "channels[0].blocks[1].content must be a string" }
    ],
    "requestId": "req_a8b0c1d2-3e4f-5678-9abc-def012345678"
  }
}
```

A platform rule refuses one thing at a time and carries `field` alone.

`500` and `503` are not the same answer. A `500` is a fault on our side and may have
half-happened; a `503` means a dependency was unreachable and the request was not
attempted. Both are worth retrying — with the same `Idempotency-Key`, which is what makes
the retry safe either way.

**New codes may be added at any time** — that is not a breaking change, so treat an
unrecognised one as a generic failure of its HTTP status rather than crashing on it.
Codes are never renamed or removed within `v1`.

`requestId` is also on every response as the `x-request-id` header and is what we search
on. Quote it and a failure is one lookup away instead of a trawl. If you already
correlate requests across your own services, send your own `x-request-id` and we will
use it.

## Platform limits

Character counts, attachments per block, thread length and whether media is mandatory
differ per platform and change when the platforms change them. `GET /platforms` serves
them live, straight from the rules this API enforces.

Read them; do not hardcode them. A client carrying its own copy of "280" will be wrong
before we are, and the failure surfaces as a rejected post rather than a stale constant.

## MCP

The same API is served to AI agents over the Model Context Protocol, at
`POST /public/v1/mcp` — streamable HTTP, authenticated by the same key, sent the
same two ways. An MCP call is an API call: same scopes, same test mode, same quota, same
rate limit.

It exposes twenty-one tools — `list_channels`, `list_platforms`,
`get_channel_capabilities`, `search_option_choices`, `list_tags`, `list_posts`,
`get_post`, `get_post_metrics`, `list_comments`, `reply_to_comment`, `create_post`,
`update_post`, `publish_post`, `revise_post`, `retract_post`, `delete_post`, `list_media`,
`upload_media_from_url`, `get_stats`, `get_posting_insights`, `get_usage` —
whose arguments are the request bodies documented here. A read-only key is shown only
the reads.

`retract_post` is the only one flagged destructive: it is the only tool here that removes
something a user can see, and nothing can undo it.

Uploading a file is absent: tool arguments are JSON, so an agent fetches media from a
public URL with `upload_media_from_url`, references media already in the library, or
leaves posting the bytes to `POST /media`.

### Connecting

Two ways, and which one you use depends on what the client can do.

**OAuth** — paste the endpoint into a client that supports remote MCP servers. It discovers
the authorization server from a `WWW-Authenticate` header on the 401, registers itself
(RFC 7591), and sends the user here to approve a workspace. No key is ever typed, and the
person who approved it can disconnect the app from the MCP screen in the app. PKCE (S256) is
required, refresh tokens rotate, and both a replayed code and a replayed refresh token revoke
the authorization outright.

**An API key** — for a client that takes a header instead of a browser. In Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http bulkit https://your-host/public/v1/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer bk_live_..."
```

## Deleting and retracting

These are different calls and neither can be recovered from the other.

`DELETE /posts/{id}` removes **our** record and leaves the published copies live. It is
the one to call to tidy a list or forget a submission.

`POST /posts/{id}/retract` deletes the copies **on their platforms**, then removes our
record of the channels that came down. It is permanent: the posts go with their likes,
their replies and their URLs. Not every channel can be retracted, so it always answers
`200` with `removed` and `remaining` rather than a bare success — read both, and read
`manageStatus` on `GET /channels` before promising a user a post can be recalled.

`POST /posts/{id}/revise` rewrites live copy in place. Use it instead of `PUT /posts/{id}`
once a submission has published; what each platform will change is `limits.remoteEdit`
on `GET /platforms`, and no platform will change a published post’s attachments.

## Versioning

The version is in the path (`/public/v1`) and a v2 would be a second prefix served
alongside this one, never a change to it. Within v1 we may add routes, add response
fields and add error codes; we will not remove or rename them, or change what an
existing field means.

Write clients that ignore unknown fields.

tags.name: Posts
tags.description: Create, schedule, inspect and publish submissions. One submission is one thing sent to one or more channels.

tags.name: Channels
tags.description: The social accounts this workspace has connected.

tags.name: Platforms
tags.description: What each supported platform accepts. Read your limits from here rather than hardcoding them.

tags.name: Media
tags.description: The media library that a post’s attachments come from.

tags.name: Tags
tags.description: The workspace’s own labels for its submissions. Ours, not any platform’s — a tag is never published. Read-only here: tags are a human’s filing system and are managed in the app.

tags.name: Stats
tags.description: Publishing analytics — what went out, when, and to which channel. Counted from the posts themselves, so unlike Usage these figures change when you delete a post. Not a billing source.

tags.name: Webhooks
tags.description: Be told what happened instead of polling for it. Publishing is asynchronous, so the outcome of every post arrives here — signed, retried, and with a delivery record you can audit.

baseUrl.description: Scheme and host of the Bulkit deployment you were given a key for. Bulkit is self-hostable, so there is no single public host to hardcode.

ApiKeyHeader.name: x-api-key
ApiKeyHeader.description: Your API key. Keys are minted in the app under **API** and shown exactly once.

BearerToken.description: The same key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Equivalent to `x-api-key` — use whichever your HTTP client makes easier.

Attachment.description: An attachment carried by one block of a post.

id.description: Media library id. The stable identifier — key durable state off this.

url.description: Short-lived download URL, minted fresh on every response. NOT a stable identifier and not safe to cache: re-read the resource instead.

altText.description: What the attachment shows, for a reader who cannot see it, or null if nobody has said. Already resolved: a description the post gave this attachment wins over the one stored on the library item, so this is the text the platforms are actually sent. Which platforms take one at all is `limits.supportsAltText` on GET /platforms; a platform that does not simply ignores it.
altText.example: A hand-drawn logo on a pale background

id.description: Use this as `channels[].channelId` when creating a post.

username.description: Handle, where the platform has one.

needsReconnect.description: True when this account can no longer publish without a human re-authorizing it. Check it before scheduling: a post to a channel in this state is accepted and then fails at publish time.

metricsStatus.description:
Whether engagement figures are collected for this channel.

`reporting` — they are, and `GET /public/v1/stats` carries them. `needs-reconnect` — the platform reports engagement but this connection was authorized before the read permission was requested; only the account owner re-authorizing in the app grants it, and no API call can. `unsupported` — the platform does not report engagement to this API at all.

Read it before drawing a conclusion from a channel contributing no engagement to `GET /public/v1/stats`: anything other than `reporting` is a gap in COVERAGE, not a finding about the posts.

manageStatus.description:
Whether a post already published to this channel can be taken down or rewritten — what `POST /public/v1/posts/{id}/retract` and `POST /public/v1/posts/{id}/revise` can actually do here.

`available` — they can, under the permissions this connection holds. `needs-reconnect` — the platform allows it, but this connection was authorized before the permission was requested; only the account owner re-authorizing in the app grants it. `unsupported` — the platform offers no way to reach a post once it is out, so a copy published here is permanent.

Read it BEFORE telling a user a post can be recalled. This is the one field here whose false answer nobody can fix: `unsupported` is a property of the platform, not of the connection.

continuationStatus.description:
Whether this channel may publish a `blocks` entry after the first.

`available` — it may, up to `limits.maxBlocks` on `GET /public/v1/platforms`. `needs-reconnect` — the platform chains, but continuing a post needs a permission this connection was authorized before we requested it; a second block is refused with `continuation_not_granted`, and only the account owner re-authorizing in the app changes that. `unsupported` — the platform publishes one post and stops.

The pair to read with `limits.maxBlocks`: that number is the PLATFORM’s and this is the CONNECTION’s. A client trusting the first alone composes a thread that is accepted nowhere.

commentsStatus.description:
Whether the audience’s comments on this channel’s posts can be read and answered, through `GET /public/v1/posts/{id}/comments` and `POST /public/v1/posts/{id}/comments/{commentId}/replies`.

`available`: they can, under the permissions this connection holds. `needs-reconnect`: the platform allows it, but this connection was authorized before the permission was requested; only the account owner re-authorizing in the app grants it. `unsupported`: comments on this platform can’t be read through this API.

Read it before listing comments. On an `unsupported` channel there is nothing to list, which is not the same as nobody having commented.

ChannelCapabilities.description: What one connected account allows, where its platform decides per account rather than per platform. Read live from the platform: it is the best answer right now, not a promise, and the same rules are checked again when the post goes out. Where a platform declares everything up front, `options` is empty and the rest is null.

options.description: The options this account narrows, settles or lacks. An option not listed here is exactly as `GET /platforms` describes it.

choices.description: The values this account may pick, for a `choice` whose platform-level `choices` is null. Null when the account does not narrow this option.

help.description: Extra context, where the label needs it.

forcedValue.description: The account has already decided this one: send exactly this value, or the platform refuses the post. Null when the value is yours to choose.

unavailable.description: This account does not offer the field at all. Leave it empty.

required.description: This account refuses a post that leaves the field empty, where its platform does not. Many subreddits require a flair, for one.

reason.description: Why the option is settled, unavailable or required, in this account’s terms.

maxCharacters.description: What this account may write in one block, where that depends on the account (a paid X tier, for one). Null leaves the platform’s `limits.maxCharacters` standing.

media.description: Stricter media rules for this account, read field by field over the platform’s `limits.media`: a null field here leaves the platform’s own rule standing. Null when the account adds nothing.

maxDurationSeconds.description: Longest a video may run. Over it is `attachment_too_long`.

minDurationSeconds.description: Shortest a video may run, exclusive. Under it is `attachment_too_short`; a `0` here rejects only a file that measured as empty.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest accepted width ÷ height. Outside the range is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`.

maxAspectRatio.description: Highest accepted width ÷ height, measured as the video plays — rotation is already applied, so a portrait phone clip counts as portrait.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels one attachment may contain — width × height. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. Not a byte ceiling in disguise, and the reason it is worth checking before you upload: a 40 megapixel camera JPEG is only a few megabytes, so it satisfies every `maxBytes` here and is still refused. Nothing on this side resizes anything, so a picture over the cap needs saving smaller first.

durationIsPerAccount.description: True when the duration cap belongs to the connected ACCOUNT rather than the platform, so no number published here could be right for every channel — TikTok grants different creators different maximums. No endpoint will tell you the number: it's resolved when the post publishes, and an over-long video fails then with that account's real limit named in the error.

perKind.description: Rules that differ by what the file IS, where one number could not be right for both kinds — Bluesky takes a 1 MB image and a 50 MB video, and a LinkedIn post carries one document OR up to twenty images. `null` on a platform that publishes no per-kind rule. All four kinds are always present when it isn't; a `null` entry means this platform states nothing about that kind, not that it refuses it — `acceptedMimeTypes` is what says which types publish at all. Nothing here widens `maxMedia`; it only narrows it further.

image.description: What this platform allows for images specifically. Null when it publishes no rule about them.

maxCount.description: Most images one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE image may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

alone.description: True when a image may not share a post with a file of any other kind. Mixing them is `attachment_kinds_mixed`.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest width ÷ height accepted for a image, where that differs from the platform-wide `minAspectRatio` above — it REPLACES that value for this kind rather than narrowing it. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Outside it is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`. Instagram is why: a feed image publishes between 4:5 and 1.91:1 where a video publishes between 0.01:1 and 10:1.

maxAspectRatio.description: Highest width ÷ height accepted for a image, on the same terms as `minAspectRatio`.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE image may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. LinkedIn is why it sits per kind: its image API refuses anything over 36,152,320 px and its video API publishes no pixel rule at all.

video.description: What this platform allows for videos specifically. Null when it publishes no rule about them.

maxCount.description: Most videos one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE video may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

alone.description: True when a video may not share a post with a file of any other kind. Mixing them is `attachment_kinds_mixed`.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest width ÷ height accepted for a video, where that differs from the platform-wide `minAspectRatio` above — it REPLACES that value for this kind rather than narrowing it. maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE video may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. maxCount.description: Most documents one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

alone.description: True when a document may not share a post with a file of any other kind. Mixing them is `attachment_kinds_mixed`.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE document may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. LinkedIn is why it sits per kind: its image API refuses anything over 36,152,320 px and its video API publishes no pixel rule at all.

caption.description: Always null. A subtitle file is a kind the media library stores and never a kind a POST carries, so no platform has a rule about how many of them one may hold. Where a subtitle file reaches a platform is a `media` option — see YouTube’s `captionFile` — whose own `mimeTypes` and `maxBytes` are the rules that bind it.

maxCount.description: Most subtitle files one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE subtitle file may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

alone.description: True when a subtitle file may not share a post with a file of any other kind. Mixing them is `attachment_kinds_mixed`.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest width ÷ height accepted for a subtitle file, where that differs from the platform-wide `minAspectRatio` above — it REPLACES that value for this kind rather than narrowing it. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Outside it is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`. Instagram is why: a feed image publishes between 4:5 and 1.91:1 where a video publishes between 0.01:1 and 10:1.

maxAspectRatio.description: Highest width ÷ height accepted for a subtitle file, on the same terms as `minAspectRatio`.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE subtitle file may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. LinkedIn is why it sits per kind: its image API refuses anything over 36,152,320 px and its video API publishes no pixel rule at all.

perType.description: Rules for one exact MIME type, where the kind above is too coarse — `null` on a platform that publishes none, which is most of them. Keyed by the mime type as `media.mimeType` reports it. X is why it exists, and it needs every field: X takes "up to 4 photos, 1 animated GIF, or 1 video", where a GIF and a JPEG are both `image` — so the ceiling (15 MB of animation against 5 MB of still), the count and the exclusion are all facts about a type. `maxBytes` REPLACES the kind's ceiling for this file; `maxCount` is counted alongside the kind's cap rather than replacing it, since five images with one GIF among them are five of the kind and one of the type.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE file of this exact type may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`, the same error the kind ceiling raises.

maxCount.description: Most files of this exact type one post may carry. Null means only the kind cap and `maxMedia` bind. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_type`.

alone.description: True when a file of this type may not share a post with a file of any other type — its own kind included, which is what separates it from the per-kind flag. Mixing them is `attachment_types_mixed`.

noun.description: What this platform calls a file of this type in a refusal — "GIF". Null where the kind name is the right word.

account.description: Who this channel posts as, as the platform names them right now, which can differ from the name stored when it was connected. Null where the platform has nothing to add.

Comment.description: One comment on a published post, read live from the platform. Nothing is stored: a comment deleted on the platform is gone here too.

id.description: The platform’s own id for the comment, which is what the replies route takes. Opaque, and its shape differs per platform.

parentId.description: The comment this one answers, or null for a comment on the post itself. Usually null at the top of a page, but a platform that pages the conversation flat (X) can list a reply on its own when its comment is on another page; it carries that comment’s id here.

authorName.description: Display name, as the platform shows it.

authorHandle.description: The author’s handle or username, where the platform has one apart from the name.

likeCount.description: Null where the platform did not report it. Never invented as zero.

url.description: A link to the comment on the platform, where one can be built.

replies.description: Direct replies, one level deep. Always empty on a reply. Your own thread’s later blocks are never listed, on any level.

CommentPage.description: One page of comments, in the order the platform returns them.

data.description: Top-level comments, each with its direct replies.

nextCursor.description: Pass back as `cursor` for the next page. Null on the last one.

id.description: The platform’s id for the reply. A test-mode key posts nothing and answers `sandbox`.

url.description: A link to the reply on the platform, where one can be built.

content.description: The text. Optional: a block carrying `mediaIds` may omit it, which publishes the image with no caption. The per-platform ceiling is lower and comes from `GET /public/v1/platforms`; this is only the outer bound one request may carry.

mediaIds.description: Media ids from `POST /public/v1/media`, in publication order. Ownership is checked server-side — an id belonging to another workspace is refused, not silently ignored.

mediaAltText.description: What each attachment shows, for a reader who cannot see it — keyed by the media id from `mediaIds` it describes. Overrides the description stored on the library item, so the same photo can read differently here. Omit a key to publish with whatever the library says; a key naming a file this block does not attach is `alt_text_unattached`. Accepted on every platform — `limits.supportsAltText` on GET /platforms says which of them will actually send it.

example.med_2f8a: A hand-drawn logo on a pale background

items.description: One person tagged on an attachment, and where on it. Whether the coordinates are wanted is `limits.userTags.positioned` on GET /platforms — send both or neither.

username.description: The platform handle, without an `@`. A leading `@` and a pasted profile URL are stripped rather than refused. Nothing here checks that the account exists: a handle that resolves to nobody is published as a post that tags nobody, with no error anywhere.

x.description: Distance from the LEFT edge as a fraction of the width — 0.5 is the middle, whatever the picture was uploaded at. Not pixels: a fraction is what survives the platform re-encoding the file.

y.description: Distance from the TOP edge as a fraction of the height.

mediaUserTags.description: Who each attachment tags, keyed by the media id from `mediaIds` they are tagged on. READ THE OPPOSITE WAY FROM `mediaAltText` above: a description is accepted on every platform because it belongs to the file, while a handle is an account on one platform and the same characters name somebody else on the next — so this is refused as `user_tags_not_supported` on a channel whose `limits.userTags` is null, rather than accepted and dropped. That declaration also says how many one attachment may carry, which kinds of file take them, and whether a tag needs a point at all.

CreatePostBlock.description: One block of the chain. Text, attachments, or both — a block with neither is refused as `content_empty`.

CreatePostChannel.description: One channel’s version of the post. There is no shared "global text" field: a client sending the same words to four channels writes them four times, and one that wants LinkedIn to read differently costs nothing extra.

title.description: The post’s title, for channels whose platform has one — check `limits.title` on `GET /public/v1/platforms`, which also carries the real cap (this `maxLength` is only the request’s outer bound). Required to publish where that field says `required`; drafts may go without. Sending it to a platform that has no title field is `title_not_supported`.
title.example: How we cut our build time in half

postType.description: Which KIND of thing to publish here, on platforms that publish more than one — an Instagram Story rather than a post on the grid. One of the `key`s in that platform’s `postTypes` on `GET /public/v1/platforms`; omit it for the default, which is what that platform’s top-level `limits` describes. A key it does not declare is `post_type_invalid`, and sending one at all where `postTypes` is empty is `post_type_not_supported`. Read the entry’s own `limits` before composing: a Story takes one attachment against ten, publishes no caption at all, holds a video for a minute rather than fifteen, and declares none of the options a post there has.

options.description: Values for the fields that belong to this channel's platform alone — Pinterest's `link` and `board_section_id`, TikTok's `privacy_level`, X's poll answers. Keyed by the `key` of each entry in that platform's `limits.options` on `GET /public/v1/platforms`, which is also where the caps and accepted values are. A key the platform doesn't declare is `option_not_supported`, not a field we quietly drop. Send a string, unless that entry's `type` is `list` — those take an array of strings, and sending the wrong one of the two shapes is `option_invalid`. The bounds here are the request's outer limits rather than any platform's: the real `minItems`, `maxItems` and per-entry `maxCharacters` are on the declaration.

blocks.description: The chain to publish, in order. One entry is an ordinary post; more is a thread, and only on platforms whose `limits.maxBlocks` allows it.

intent.description:
What to do with it.
`draft` — store it, publish nothing. It still occupies its slot.
`schedule` — store it and start a durable timer for `scheduledAt`.
`now` — store it and queue it for immediate publication.

`now` is ASYNCHRONOUS: the response comes back with the submission `publishing`, not published. Publishing takes as long as the platforms take, and a request that blocked on it would time out on exactly the submissions that matter most.

scheduledAt.description: Required when `intent` is `schedule`. For `draft` it is the slot the post occupies; for `now` it defaults to the moment it was queued.

channels.description: Where it goes. At least one, for every intent — including drafts.

tagIds.description: The workspace’s own labels for this submission — ids from `GET /public/v1/tags`. Ids rather than names, because the name is the field a workspace edits. An id this workspace does not own is `tag_not_found`, not a value we drop. On `PUT` this is a replacement like the rest of the body, so omitting it removes every tag.

url.description: Absolute `https://` (or `http://` for a local receiver, where the deployment allows it). Addresses only reachable from inside our network are refused as `webhook_url_invalid` — nothing sent to one would reach you.

events.description: What to send here. Required and non-empty: an endpoint subscribed to nothing looks exactly like a working integration until the first event it should have received.

Error.description: The envelope every public-API failure arrives in.

code.description: What to branch on. Adding a code is NOT a breaking change, so treat an unrecognised one as a generic failure of the HTTP status rather than crashing.

message.description: The explanation, in prose, and the best one available — safe to surface to your own users. Never branch on it.
message.example: X (Twitter) allows 280 characters — this one is 300

field.description: Path into the request body that caused it, where one applies — or the name of the offending header, for the failures a header produces (`Idempotency-Key`). When `details` is present this is the first of them.

details.description: Every field that failed, when schema validation rejected more than one. Absent otherwise — a platform rule refuses one thing at a time. Fix them together rather than a round trip per mistake.

requestId.description: Echoed from the `x-request-id` response header and logged server-side. Quote it in a support request and the failure is one lookup away.

FieldError.description: One field that failed validation, and why.

message.description: Why it was rejected. Prose — never branch on it.

format.description: From the media on ANY block of the post, so a thread whose third block is a video is a video post. Video wins when a post has both.

posts.description: Posts behind `score`. Apply a floor before comparing: the app compares nothing under 5.

score.description: Average of each post’s engagement divided by its own channel’s usual. `1` is usual; `1.4` is 40% better than those accounts normally do.

hour.description: Hour of the day the post went out, in `timezone`.

IssuedWebhookEndpoint.description: An endpoint together with its signing secret. Returned by exactly two operations — registering an endpoint and rolling its secret — and by nothing else, ever.

secret.description: The signing secret, in the clear. **Store it now.** Only an encrypted copy is kept; the only way to get another is to roll it, which invalidates this one.

MediaItem.description: An item in the workspace’s media library.

id.description: Media library id. The stable identifier — key durable state off this.

url.description: Short-lived download URL, minted fresh on every response. NOT a stable identifier and not safe to cache: re-read the resource instead.

altText.description: What the attachment shows, for a reader who cannot see it, or null if nobody has said. Already resolved: a description the post gave this attachment wins over the one stored on the library item, so this is the text the platforms are actually sent. Which platforms take one at all is `limits.supportsAltText` on GET /platforms; a platform that does not simply ignores it.

MediaUpload.description: An open upload session. Cut the file into `partCount` parts of `partSize` bytes (the last one is whatever is left), ask for their URLs, PUT each part, then complete.

id.description: The upload session id. Not a media id: that comes from complete.

partSize.description: Bytes in every part but the last.

partCount.description: Parts are numbered 1 to this, inclusive.

url.description: PUT this part’s bytes here as the raw request body, with no auth header. Signed for the part’s exact length and valid for an hour, so ask for URLs as you go rather than all at once.

OptionChoices.description: The matching values, best first. Empty when nothing matches.

help.description: Extra context, where the label needs it.

Platform.description: A supported platform and everything it will accept.

name.description: Human name, e.g. "X". Display only — never branch on it.

postTypes.description: The KINDS of thing this platform publishes, where it publishes more than one — an Instagram Story against a post on the grid. EMPTY on every platform with a single kind, which is all of them but Instagram, so there is always an array to read. Send one entry’s `key` as `channels[].postType`; a key that is not listed is `post_type_invalid`, and sending one at all where this array is empty is `post_type_not_supported`. Omitting it asks for the FIRST entry, which is what `limits` above already describes — so a client that ignores this field reads exactly the platform it read before post types existed.

continuationNoun.description: What this platform calls a block after the first: "post" on X, "comment" on LinkedIn. Travels so your own error messages can use the word your user would recognise.

PlatformLimits.description: What this platform accepts. Read these rather than hardcoding them — they change when a platform changes, and a client carrying its own copy will be wrong before we are.

maxCharactersPerAccount.description: The most a block may carry on an account with the platform's paid tier, where one buys more room than `maxCharacters`. Null where every account gets the same number, which is every platform but X. Compose against `maxCharacters` unless you know the account has paid: nothing here says which tier a channel is on, so text between the two numbers is accepted by this API and settled by the platform at publish — it goes out for an account that pays and comes back as a publish error for one that doesn't. Over this number is `content_too_long`, for anyone.

urlWeight.description: What ONE LINK costs against `maxCharacters`, on a platform that rewrites every URL to a shortener of its own. Null where a link costs its own length, which is every platform but X. Count with this before deciding text is too long: X charges 23 for any link, so a post that looks 60 characters over can be comfortably under.

maxMedia.description: Attachments the first block may carry. 0 means the platform takes none.

maxMediaOnContinuation.description: Attachments a block AFTER the first may carry. Equal to `maxMedia` where position makes no difference; always present, so a client never implements the fallback itself.

maxReplyCharacters.description: Characters a reply to a comment may carry, where that differs from a post. Null where a reply is held to `maxCharacters` and `maxCharactersPerAccount` like a post. Over it is `content_too_long`.

maxBlocks.description: Blocks one submission may chain. `1` means this platform has no threads. The PLATFORM’s number: a channel whose `continuationStatus` on `GET /public/v1/channels` is not `available` is capped at one block whatever this says, so read the two together before composing a thread.

requiresMedia.description: The platform refuses a post carrying no attachment at all.

acceptedMimeTypes.description: The mime types an attachment may be on this platform. The counts above can't express this, and on a video-only platform it decides whether the post can go out at all — check an upload's `mimeType` against every platform it's headed for.

supportsAltText.description: This platform publishes a per-attachment description and we send it. NOT a rule to validate against — `blocks[].mediaAltText` is accepted on every platform, because a description belongs to the file and one submission fans out to several channels. Read it to decide whether to ask for a description, and to explain why the one you wrote will not appear on a channel that returns false.

userTags.description: What this platform does with people tagged on an attachment, or null when it tags nobody. UNLIKE `supportsAltText` above, this IS a rule to validate against: a description belongs to the file and an unused one costs the post nothing, while a handle is an account on THIS platform and the same characters name somebody else on the next one — so `blocks[].mediaUserTags` sent to a channel whose value here is null is refused as `user_tags_not_supported`. The whole object changes with `channels[].postType`; read it off the entry in `postTypes` you are publishing.

maxItems.description: Most people ONE attachment may tag. Per attachment, not per post: a carousel tags this many on every picture it carries.

kinds.description: Which kinds of attachment take a tag. Tagging a file of any other kind is `user_tags_kind_unsupported`.

positioned.description: A tag names a POINT on the attachment as well as a person. Send `x` and `y` when true and neither when false — either one the wrong way round is `user_tag_position_invalid`. An Instagram feed photo is true; a Story is false, because it mentions someone without pointing at them.

publishesContent.description: This platform publishes the block's text. `false` means it has no caption field at all — an Instagram Story, where the words are stored, published on every other channel of the same submission, and dropped here. Not a rule to check against: content is accepted on every platform, because one submission fans out to several and a caption written for four channels is not refused by the fifth. Where it is false there is nothing to count against `maxCharacters`.

title.description: Set on platforms whose post has a TITLE field of its own, alongside its body — send it as `channels[].title` when creating a post. `null` on platforms that have no such field, which is most of them; sending a title to one of those is rejected with `title_not_supported` rather than ignored. Where it is set, `maxCharacters` is the title's own cap (unrelated to `maxCharacters` above, which measures the body) and going over is `title_too_long` — the title is never silently shortened. If `required` is true, publishing without one is `title_required`; drafts are exempt.

maxCharacters.description: Characters the title may carry. Counted in code points, so an emoji is one character.

label.description: What the platform calls the field. Display only — never branch on it.

required.description: The platform will not publish a post without a title. Checked when publishing, not when drafting.

standsAlone.description: A first block carrying a title needs nothing else — no `content`, no `mediaIds`. True on Reddit, where a link submission is a title and a URL and a self post with an empty body is an ordinary title-only post. False everywhere else, where a block with neither text nor an attachment is `content_empty` whatever its title says. Only the first block: a continuation has no title of its own.

options.description: Fields this platform has that others don't — Pinterest's destination link and alt text, TikTok's privacy level. Send values as `channels[].options`, keyed by each entry's `key`. Empty on a platform whose post is only its content, so there is always an array here to read. A key that isn't listed is rejected with `option_not_supported` rather than dropped.

key.description: Send the value under this key in `channels[].options`.

label.description: What the platform calls the field. Display only — never branch on it.

type.description: `text` is free text capped by `maxCharacters`; `url` must be an absolute http(s) address or it is `option_invalid`; `choice` must be one of `choices` when that list is present; `boolean` takes the string `"true"` or `"false"`; `media` is the id of a file you uploaded, and the `media` object on this entry says what that file may be. Those five are all sent as strings whatever they mean. `list` is the one that is not: it is a REPEATED value — X’s poll answers — sent as a JSON array of strings, bounded by `minItems`/`maxItems`, with `maxCharacters` applying to each entry rather than to the whole. `search` is a string too, and it is an opaque platform id from a set too large to publish here — Instagram’s `location_id` is one Facebook Page out of every Page that has an address. Its `choices` is null and stays null, because there is no list. Send an id you already hold and nothing validates it on submission; the platform settles it when the post goes out, which for a place that has since closed is the post publishing without one. To turn a NAME into one of these ids, call `GET /channels/{id}/options/{key}/choices?q=...` and send the `value` it returns.

required.description: The platform will not publish without this field. Checked when publishing, not when drafting — going without is `option_required`.

help.description: A sentence describing the field, where its label doesn't say enough on its own.

helpWhenOn.description: Shown in place of `help` while a `boolean` is on — the sentence that only becomes true once it's set. Where a platform requires a declaration before publishing, this is it: TikTok's guidelines set out what a creator undertakes by marking a video a paid partnership, and a client that puts someone in front of that checkbox is expected to put them in front of this too. Null on every non-boolean and on every option with nothing extra to say.

maxCharacters.description: Cap for a `text` or `url`, counted in code points, and for ONE ENTRY of a `list`. Over it is `option_too_long` — the value is never silently shortened — and on a list the error’s `field` pointer carries the index of the entry that was too long. The per-entry reading is the only one that means anything on a repeated field: X allows 25 characters per poll answer and states no rule about the four of them together. Null on a `choice`.

minItems.description: Fewest entries a `list` may carry, checked only when publishing — like `required`, because a draft carrying one poll answer so far is unfinished rather than wrong. Under it is `option_too_few`. An EMPTY list is not this: it is the same as sending nothing at all, so it answers to `required` and never to `minItems`. Null on every other type, and on a list the platform does not bound from below.

maxItems.description: Most entries a `list` may carry, checked whenever the field is sent. Over it is `option_too_many` — separate from `option_too_long`, which on a list measures one entry, because too many answers and too long an answer are fixed in different places. Null on every other type.

media.description: What a `media` option's file may be — a SECOND attachment, with rules of its own rather than the block's. Deliberately not `acceptedMimeTypes` and `limits.media`, which describe the post's attachments: a YouTube post's attachment is the video and its thumbnail is a still picture, and the same platform refuses each in the other's place. Send the media `id` as this option's value, exactly as `blocks[].mediaIds` takes ids. A file that isn't in your workspace, isn't one of `mimeTypes`, or is over `maxBytes` is `option_invalid` against this key. Null on every other type.

mimeTypes.description: The file types this slot publishes. What our publish SENDS today rather than what the platform documents — the same promise `acceptedMimeTypes` makes.

maxBytes.description: Byte ceiling for this one file, or null where the platform publishes none.

choices.description: The accepted values of a `choice` — or **null when they depend on the connected account rather than the platform**, which is TikTok's privacy levels: what a creator may post as varies by account and by the app's review status, so no list published here would be right for every channel. A null means the value isn't validated on submission; read what one channel allows from `GET /channels/{id}/capabilities`, or send what the account should use and the platform settles it at publish time, falling back to what that account does allow. Always null on a `text` or `url`, and always null on a `search` for a different reason worth telling apart: a dynamic `choice` has a list this endpoint can't publish because it belongs to an account, while a `search` has no list at all.

help.description: Extra context, where the label needs it.

rulesOut.description: What this field rules out elsewhere, read as: while you send a value for this key, the named option may not carry the listed values — or, where `values` is null, may not carry any value at all. “Sending a value” is the same reading `rulesOutMedia` uses: a `boolean` counts only as `"true"`, a `list` only with an entry in it. A rule of the platform's rather than of ours — TikTok will not publish a video marked as a paid partnership with a `privacy_level` of `SELF_ONLY`, and Threads will not attach a link preview to a post that is also a poll — and sending the pair anyway is `option_invalid` against the key named here, not against the field that caused it. This is the one case where a `choice` with a null `choices` list is validated on submission: what an account may pick is still not checked, but a combination the platform publishes as impossible needs nothing asked of the account. A MUTUAL exclusion appears on both fields, each carrying the sentence that reads correctly when that field is the one you added. Always an array; empty on the options that have no such rule, which is most of them.

values.description: Values of that option you may not send alongside this one, or null where the option may not be sent at all — the only reading available where the other field has no enumerable values (a `text`, a `url` or a `list`). Never an empty array: a rule that excludes nothing is not published.

reason.description: Why, in the platform's terms. Safe to show a user verbatim.

rulesOutMedia.description: Set where sending a value for this field means the post may carry NO ATTACHMENTS, to the platform’s own sentence saying why — safe to show a user verbatim. `rulesOut`’s counterpart for the thing a post HAS rather than a field it carries: a tweet is a poll or it is pictures, never both. Sending the pair anyway is `option_invalid`, reported against the `mediaIds` of the block that would have to give something up rather than against this key. Applies while the field has any value at all — a `boolean` that is `"true"`, or a `list` with an entry in it; an empty list rules nothing out. Null where the field and the attachments are independent, which is nearly everywhere.

requires.description: What sending a value for this field makes REQUIRED elsewhere: while this one carries a value, every option named here has to carry one too. `rulesOut`’s obligation to its prohibition, and it exists because `required` cannot say it — LinkedIn’s poll needs a question as well as its answers, and declaring the question `required` would demand one of every ordinary status update. “Carrying a value” is the same reading the two rules above use: a `boolean` counts only as `"true"`, a `list` only with an entry in it. Sending one half without the other is `option_required` against the key named here — the same code as a plain missing field, because that is what it is, with the platform’s own sentence in place of ours. Checked only when publishing, like `required` and `minItems`: a draft carrying half a poll is unfinished rather than wrong. A MUTUAL obligation appears on both fields, each carrying the sentence that reads correctly when that field is the half you left out. Always an array; empty on the options that impose nothing, which is nearly all of them.

key.description: The other option's `key` — the one you also have to send a value for.

reason.description: Why, in the platform's terms. Safe to show a user verbatim, and it names both repairs: send the missing half, or clear the one you sent.

requiredWithMedia.description: Set where an ATTACHMENT of one kind makes this field necessary, to that kind and the platform’s own sentence saying why. `requires` read from the other side — there another FIELD makes this one necessary, here it is a file: Pinterest refuses a Pin made from a video that has no cover image, and `required` could not say so, since most Pins are pictures and a picture has no cover. Checked only when publishing, like `required` and `requires`, and refused as `option_required` against this key rather than against the attachment that caused it. Null where nothing a post carries has any bearing on the field, which is nearly everywhere.

kind.description: The kind of attachment that makes this field necessary — the same vocabulary `media.perKind` is keyed by. An attachment of any other kind leaves the field optional. `caption` is in the vocabulary and cannot appear here: a subtitle file is never a post’s attachment.

reason.description: Why, in the platform's terms. Safe to show a user verbatim, and it names both repairs: fill this field in, or attach something else.

revealedBy.description: The `boolean` option that has to be on before this field may carry a value at all. A FOLLOW-UP QUESTION rather than a rule between two answers, which is what separates it from `rulesOut` and `requires`: those describe what a filled-in field does to another field that is always there, while this says the field is not there yet. TikTok’s commercial-content disclosure is the case — the two boxes naming what a post promotes only mean anything once the creator has said it promotes something. Sending a value for this key while the named option is off or absent is `option_invalid` against THIS key, and it is refused whether or not you are publishing: it is not an unfinished answer, it is an answer to a question nobody asked. On TikTok it is also a commercial label, and a label nobody confirmed must not reach a published video. Null where the field always applies, which is nearly everywhere.

requiresAnyOf.description: `requires` with the quantifier changed: while this field carries a value, ANY ONE of the named options has to carry one too. That rule names a field and demands it, and two entries mean both; this names a set and demands one of them without preferring either. TikTok’s disclosure parent is the case — the creator has to say which kind of promotion it is, and either answer is a complete one. Checked only when publishing, like `required` and `requires`, and refused as `option_required` against the first key in the set. Null where the field demands nothing, which is nearly everywhere.

keys.description: The option keys, one of which must carry a value. “Carrying a value” is the same reading every other rule here uses: a `boolean` counts only as `"true"`, a `list` only with an entry in it.

reason.description: Why, in the platform's terms. Safe to show a user verbatim, and it names both repairs: answer one of them, or clear the field that asked.

media.description: What an attachment must BE here beyond its file type — how long a video runs and what shape it is. `null` on a platform that publishes no such rule, which is most of them. Every field is transcribed from the platform's own spec and nothing is inferred, so a null field means the platform states no rule rather than that anything goes. Worth reading before you upload rather than before you post: these are the limits you can only satisfy with a different file. Checked only against values we measured — duration and dimensions are read from the container at upload, are always unknown for images, and an unknown value never refuses a post.

maxDurationSeconds.description: Longest a video may run. Over it is `attachment_too_long`.

minDurationSeconds.description: Shortest a video may run, exclusive. Under it is `attachment_too_short`; a `0` here rejects only a file that measured as empty.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest accepted width ÷ height. Outside the range is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`.

maxAspectRatio.description: Highest accepted width ÷ height, measured as the video plays — rotation is already applied, so a portrait phone clip counts as portrait.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels one attachment may contain — width × height. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. Not a byte ceiling in disguise, and the reason it is worth checking before you upload: a 40 megapixel camera JPEG is only a few megabytes, so it satisfies every `maxBytes` here and is still refused. Nothing on this side resizes anything, so a picture over the cap needs saving smaller first.

durationIsPerAccount.description: True when the duration cap belongs to the connected ACCOUNT rather than the platform, so no number published here could be right for every channel — TikTok grants different creators different maximums. No endpoint will tell you the number: it's resolved when the post publishes, and an over-long video fails then with that account's real limit named in the error.

perKind.description: Rules that differ by what the file IS, where one number could not be right for both kinds — Bluesky takes a 1 MB image and a 50 MB video, and a LinkedIn post carries one document OR up to twenty images. `null` on a platform that publishes no per-kind rule. All four kinds are always present when it isn't; a `null` entry means this platform states nothing about that kind, not that it refuses it — `acceptedMimeTypes` is what says which types publish at all. Nothing here widens `maxMedia`; it only narrows it further.

image.description: What this platform allows for images specifically. Null when it publishes no rule about them.

maxCount.description: Most images one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE image may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

alone.description: True when a image may not share a post with a file of any other kind. Mixing them is `attachment_kinds_mixed`.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest width ÷ height accepted for a image, where that differs from the platform-wide `minAspectRatio` above — it REPLACES that value for this kind rather than narrowing it. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Outside it is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`. Instagram is why: a feed image publishes between 4:5 and 1.91:1 where a video publishes between 0.01:1 and 10:1.

maxAspectRatio.description: Highest width ÷ height accepted for a image, on the same terms as `minAspectRatio`.

maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE image may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. LinkedIn is why it sits per kind: its image API refuses anything over 36,152,320 px and its video API publishes no pixel rule at all.

video.description: What this platform allows for videos specifically. Null when it publishes no rule about them.

maxCount.description: Most videos one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE video may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

Null means the platform-wide one applies. Outside it is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`. maxPixels.description: Most pixels ONE video may contain — width × height — where that differs from the platform-wide `maxPixels` above, which it REPLACES for this kind rather than narrowing. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Over it is `attachment_too_many_pixels`. LinkedIn is why it sits per kind: its image API refuses anything over 36,152,320 px and its video API publishes no pixel rule at all.

maxCount.description: Most documents one post may carry, where that is tighter than `maxMedia`. Null means only `maxMedia` binds. Over it is `too_many_attachments_of_kind`.

maxBytes.description: Largest ONE document may be, in bytes. Over it is `attachment_too_large`. The only media rule checked on every attachment — a stored file always has a size, where the duration and dimensions above are measured best-effort and are unknown for every image.

minAspectRatio.description: Lowest width ÷ height accepted for a document, where that differs from the platform-wide `minAspectRatio` above — it REPLACES that value for this kind rather than narrowing it. Null means the platform-wide one applies. Outside it is `attachment_aspect_unsupported`. Instagram is why: a feed image publishes between 4:5 and 1.91:1 where a video publishes between 0.01:1 and 10:1.
